paragraphs.text: Camptodactyly, impaired intellectual development, and facial dysmorphism syndrome (CIDFS) is a neurodevelopmental malformation syndrome. Ufartes et al. (2020) described respiratory insufficiency, feeding difficulties, postnatal growth restriction, microcephaly, global developmental delay with no active speech, contractures, and facial dysmorphism. Some patients also had heart defects, cleft palate, and distinctive skin creases in the first year of life. The phenotype overlaps with the severe form of AUTS2 syndrome but appears to include a wider range of congenital malformations (Pauli et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Ufartes et al. (2020) reported 3 unrelated children with a recognizable malformation syndrome. Patients 1 and 2 had a nearly identical phenotype. In the first year of life they had respiratory insufficiency, feeding difficulties, postnatal growth restriction, microcephaly, global developmental delay, no active speech, contractures, heart defects, cleft palate, facial dysmorphism, and distinctive skin creases. The skin creases were most pronounced immediately after birth and regressed with age. Ufartes et al. (2020) noted that, unlike in congenital symmetric circumferential skin creases syndrome, the back rather than the arms and legs was preferentially affected. In patient 2, the skin folds had regressed markedly by age 2.5 years. Facial features included a pronounced neck fold, flat occiput, and dysmorphic auricles; patient 2 also had deep-set eyes, a round face, and temporal indentations. All 3 patients had intellectual disability or global developmental delay, delayed speech, autistic behavior, microcephaly, swallowing difficulty, postnatal growth retardation, skeletal abnormalities, camptodactyly/contractures, facial dysmorphism, and respiratory failure requiring ventilation therapy. Patient 1 had atrial septal defect (ASD) and patent ductus arteriosus, and patient 2 had ASD and ventricular septal defect. Patients 1 and 2 had cleft palate and hearing impairment. Patient 2 had asplenia and patient 1 had an anal abnormality. Patient 3, photographed at 12 years 6 months and 14 years 8 months, had contractures of both hands and fingers and widely spaced teeth, and had no heart defect, cleft palate, or skin creases.

paragraphs.text: Pauli et al. (2021) reviewed the 3 patients of Ufartes et al. (2020) and compared them with AUTS2 syndrome patients using the AUTS2 syndrome severity scoring system. All 3 patients had short stature, microcephaly, feeding difficulties, intellectual disability, autistic behavior, kyphosis/scoliosis, camptodactyly/contractures, and respiratory insufficiency requiring ventilation therapy. Two of the 3 had low birth weight, cerebral palsy/spasticity, high arched eyebrows, epicanthal folds, a deep or broad nasal bridge, a short or upturned philtrum, low-set ears, and widely spaced teeth. One patient had anal atresia. Pauli et al. (2021) described the congenital skin creases of the 2 more severely affected patients as involving the back, arms, and legs, disappearing during the first year of life. They concluded that patients with FBRSL1 variants had a higher rate and wider spectrum of congenital malformations than patients with AUTS2 syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bukvic et al. (2024) reported an Italian girl, the third child of healthy nonconsanguineous parents. The pregnancy was complicated by threatened miscarriage and poor fetal movements. At term birth she weighed 2,860 g (less than 10th centile) and measured 39.5 cm in length (less than 3rd centile), and her head circumference was 34 cm. She had neonatal feeding difficulties due to weak sucking and postnatal growth retardation. Skeletal findings included bilateral contractures of the hands and fingers, bilateral congenital hip dislocation, and irregular growth fronts of the long bones. She was initially diagnosed with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita at 4 months of age. Developmental delay was global: she achieved head control at 7 months, sat without support at 14 months, and walked without support at 46 months. At 48 months she had no active speech and severe intellectual disability (developmental quotient 22), microcephaly (head circumference 45.3 cm, -2.68 SD), and motor stereotypies. Facial dysmorphism included flat occiput, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, short philtrum, micrognathia, and microstomia with a 'whistling mouth.' She also had mild scoliosis and slight distal hypertonia of the legs with supinated, varus feet. Hearing was normal and there was no heart defect. Cerebral and spinal MRI at 2 months and 4 years and metabolic studies were normal. From 46 months she had daily drop tonic seizures, later with myoclonic absences. Interictal EEG showed frontocentral spikes and spike-and-wave complexes. Bukvic et al. (2024) reported that no autism spectrum disorder was found, although their comparison table listed autism/autistic behavior as present. Gastrostomy was performed at 6 years of age because of feeding difficulties and poor weight gain. Unlike the patients of Ufartes et al. (2020), she lacked skin creases, cleft palate, heart defects, hearing impairment, and respiratory insufficiency.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated children with CIDFS, Ufartes et al. (2020) identified heterozygous truncating mutations in the FBRSL1 gene. In patients 1 and 2, trio exome sequencing excluded pathogenic variants in TUBB, MAPRE2, and AUTS2. Patient 1 carried a de novo c.487C-T transition predicting a gln163-to-ter (Q163X) substitution, and Sanger sequencing confirmed that it was absent in both unaffected parents. In patient 2, no change was initially found in the annotated FBRSL1 transcript. Manual inspection of intronic reads then revealed a 23-bp deletion that affected an alternative exon 3 of a then-hypothetical short N-terminal transcript (c.581_603del). Sanger sequencing showed that the deletion was de novo. In patient 3, single exome sequencing and reverse phenotyping identified a c.332G-A transition predicting a trp111-to-ter (W111X) substitution. This mutation was not found in the mother, and the father was unavailable for testing. None of the variants was present in gnomAD or ExAC. RNA analysis showed that all 3 truncating variants escaped nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Ufartes et al. (2020) showed by RT-PCR and Western blot that short N-terminal FBRSL1 isoforms (3.1 and 3.2) containing a DNA translocase (FtsK) domain exist, and all 3 mutations affected these isoforms.

(2020) noted that the long FBRSL1 isoform 1 appears tolerant to loss-of-function variants (pLI = 0.01 in gnomAD), so haploinsufficiency of the long transcripts seemed unlikely. paragraphs.text: In a girl (patient 2) with CIDFS, Ufartes et al. (2020) identified a de novo heterozygous 23-bp deletion in the FBRSL1 gene by manually inspecting intronic reads from trio exome sequencing. The deletion lies in an alternative exon 3 of the short N-terminal transcript (isoform 3.1; XM_005266181.4) and is described as c.581_603del relative to that transcript. It was predicted to cause a frameshift with a premature stop codon at position 356 of isoform 3.1, disrupting the DNA translocase domain, while isoform 1 was unaffected. Sanger sequencing confirmed the deletion in the patient and wildtype sequence in her healthy parents. RT-PCR of lymphocyte cDNA confirmed the heterozygous deletion at the transcript level.

agent.process_note: I read the full texts of Ufartes et al. (2020), Pauli et al. (2021) and Bukvic et al. (2024), and the abstract of Xu et al. (2026), which is the only part available. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the intro gives no MIM number or cytogenetic band for FBRSL1. 'Chromosome 12' comes from the GRCh37 coordinates in Ufartes et al. (2020). For the Xu et al. (2026) variant the abstract gives only the protein change (p.Ala128Cysfs*5), not the nucleotide change, and gives no details on the other patients in their 4-patient analysis. The sex of patients 1 and 3 of Ufartes et al. (2020) is not stated, so I did not report it. The papers disagree on two points. On skin crease distribution, Ufartes et al. say mainly the back, while Pauli et al. say the back, arms, and legs. On autism in the Bukvic patient, the text says none was found, but the comparison table marks it as present. I described both disagreements rather than resolving them.
